---
title: "Events"
---

The pronoun sample space lists individual forms, but most linguistic questions concern properties shared by several forms. If we ask whether a recorded pronoun is third person, *he*, *her*, and *them* give the same answer. An event groups these outcomes without treating the forms themselves as identical.

An [**event**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is a set of outcomes. Let $T$ be the event that the recorded pronoun is third person:

$$
T
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The event $T$ occurs exactly when the realized outcome belongs to this set. Thus $T$ occurs when the outcome is *him* but not when the outcome is *we*. An outcome is one possible result, whereas an event is a set of results that make a proposition true.

The same outcome may belong to many events. That fact lets us represent several properties of one token.

## Events defined by linguistic properties

Let $A$ be the event that the pronoun has accusative form:

$$
A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{us},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The forms *him*, *her*, and *them* belong to both $T$ and $A$. We can represent the question “is the pronoun both third person and accusative?” by keeping only those shared outcomes. The relevant operation is intersection:

$$
T\cap A
=\{\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The expression $T\cap A$ is read as “$T$ and $A$.” An outcome belongs to the intersection only if it satisfies both descriptions.

Now ask whether the pronoun is third person or accusative. We keep every outcome that belongs to at least one of the events. The relevant operation is union:

$$
T\cup A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},
\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The expression $T\cup A$ is read as “$T$ or $A$,” where *or* is inclusive. The outcome *him* belongs to the union even though it belongs to both events.

Finally, suppose we ask whether the pronoun is not third person. The complement $T^c$ contains every outcome in $\Omega$ that is not in $T$:

$$
T^c
=\{\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{we},\textit{us}\}.
$$

The complement is always relative to the declared sample space. If $\Omega$ included reflexive pronouns, then $T^c$ might include additional forms.

## Event membership

Take the outcome *them*.

1. *them* belongs to $T$, so the third person event occurs.
2. *them* belongs to $A$, so the accusative event occurs.
3. *them* belongs to $T\cap A$, since both events occur.
4. *them* does not belong to $T^c$, since the third person event occurs.

Now take *me*. It belongs to $A$ but not $T$. It thus belongs to $T\cup A$, but not to $T\cap A$.

Base R supplies operations with the same interpretation.

```{r}
#| eval: false
omega <- c("I", "me", "you", "he", "him", "she", "her",
           "we", "us", "they", "them")
third <- c("he", "him", "she", "her", "they", "them")
accusative <- c("me", "him", "her", "us", "them")

intersect(third, accusative)
union(third, accusative)
setdiff(omega, third)
```

The final expression computes $T^c$ by removing the members of $T$ from $\Omega$.

## The two limiting events

The empty event $\varnothing$ contains no outcomes. It cannot occur under the current representation. The full event $\Omega$ contains every outcome, so it occurs whenever the observation process produces a represented result.

These are events because both are subsets of $\Omega$. They will provide the lower and upper endpoints when we assign probabilities.

## Set operations and linguistic interpretation

Translate each linguistic connective into the corresponding set operation. If we translate *and* with a union, or inclusive *or* with an intersection, we answer a different question.

Consider the claim “the pronoun is plural and accusative.” A union would include plural nominative *they* and singular accusative *him*. Those forms satisfy only half of the claim. The intersection retains only *them*, which satisfies both parts.

Complements also change when the sample space changes. If we compute $T^c$ relative to personal pronouns and later interpret it relative to all noun phrases, we have changed which outcomes belong to the complement. Write $\Omega$ before computing a complement so that the reference set remains visible.

## Check your understanding

1. Write $T\setminus A$, the third person outcomes that are not accusative. Then verify that $(T\cap A)\cup(T\setminus A)=T$.
2. Let $P=\{\textit{we},\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}$ be the plural event. List $P\cap A$ and $P\cup A$.
3. Explain why *them* can make both $T$ and $A$ occur without being two outcomes.
4. Suppose reflexives are added to $\Omega$. Which part of the definition of $T^c$ must be recomputed?

Events give us the questions we might ask. A probability model must also state which of those questions it is prepared to measure. The [next page](event-spaces.qmd) introduces that collection.
